13960: The Millennium and the End of History
13961: How should we read Revelation 20 and the end of history?
13962:
Revelation 20:1-10 describes Satan bound for a thousand years, martyrs and faithful believers who come to life and reign with Christ, a release of Satan, a last rebellion and a final judgment. It is the only passage in Scripture that names a thousand-year period, yet how it is read shapes a whole picture of history: whether Christ's kingdom is mainly future or already present, whether the world will get worse or better before he returns, what becomes of the promises to Israel, and whether much of biblical prophecy has already been fulfilled.

The classic labels describe where Christ's return falls relative to the millennium. Premillennialists (in historic and dispensational forms) expect Christ to return before an earthly thousand-year reign. Amillennialists read the thousand years as a symbol of the present age between Christ's first and second comings. Postmillennialists expect Christ to return after a long age of gospel triumph. Cutting across these, preterists (partial and full) argue that much or all of New Testament prophecy was fulfilled in the first century, especially the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, and idealists read Revelation as a symbolic portrayal of the conflict between Christ and evil throughout the church age.

These are interpretive approaches held by serious Christians across the centuries. The text itself states the binding, the reign, the release and the judgment; the order, timing and literalness of these events are the matter of debate.
13964:
Dispensational premillennialism holds that Christ will return before a literal thousand-year kingdom on earth, centered in Jerusalem, in which God fulfills his unconditional promises to the nation of Israel. It reads prophecy with a consistent literal (grammatical-historical) method and draws a clear distinction between God's program for Israel and his program for the church.

In its classic form, the church age is a parenthesis not foreseen in Old Testament prophecy. It ends with a pretribulation rapture, after which Daniel's seventieth week unfolds as a seven-year tribulation focused on Israel. Christ then returns visibly, binds Satan, and reigns for a thousand years before the final rebellion, the last judgment and the eternal state. Progressive dispensationalists (from the 1980s) soften the Israel-church divide and see the Davidic kingdom as already inaugurated, while still expecting a future earthly kingdom with a restored Israel.

13975:
Dispensationalism emerged in the British Brethren movement amid a wave of prophetic interest following the French Revolution, including the Albury (1826-1830) and Powerscourt (1831-1833) prophecy conferences. It crossed to North America through Darby's travels, the Niagara Bible Conferences (from 1878), and Bible institutes such as Moody and later Dallas Theological Seminary (1924).

It offered a reading of Scripture that took Old Testament promises at face value, a defense of biblical authority against liberal theology, and a framework for current events. The founding of the State of Israel in 1948 was widely seen by its adherents as confirmation. Through the Scofield Bible, prophecy conferences, Hal Lindsey's books and the Left Behind novels, it became the most widely held popular eschatology among American evangelicals in the twentieth century.

14036:
Historic premillennialism holds that Christ will return after a period of tribulation that the church passes through, raise the righteous dead, and then reign on earth for a thousand years (or an extended period) before the final resurrection, judgment and new creation. It is called historic because a form of it was held by several important second-century writers, including Papias, Justin Martyr and Irenaeus.

Unlike dispensationalism, it does not separate the destinies of Israel and the church sharply, does not require a pretribulation rapture, and typically reads the Old Testament through New Testament fulfillment. Its modern defenders, led by George Eldon Ladd, combine an already-and-not-yet view of the kingdom with the conviction that Revelation 20 describes a stage of Christ's victory that follows his return.

14039: Papias collected oral traditions from those who had heard the apostles and elders. Irenaeus preserves his report of a coming kingdom of extraordinary fruitfulness, and Eusebius, who disliked his millenarianism, called him a man of limited understanding. His five-book work survives only in fragments.

14047:
Early Christian millenarianism (chiliasm, from the Greek for thousand) flourished in Asia Minor in the second century, drawing on Jewish hopes for a messianic kingdom and on Revelation. Irenaeus used it against Gnostic contempt for matter. From the third century, Alexandrian theologians such as Origen criticized literalistic hopes, and after Augustine the amillennial reading dominated the West.

Premillennialism revived among some Protestants in the seventeenth century (for example Joseph Mede) and again in the nineteenth. In the twentieth century Ladd and others presented historic premillennialism as an evangelical alternative to dispensationalism, and it has wide support among New Testament scholars who read Rev 20 as following Rev 19 sequentially.

14105:
Amillennialism (sometimes called realized millennialism) reads the thousand years of Revelation 20 as a symbolic description of the whole period between Christ's first and second comings. Satan was bound by Christ's victory so that he cannot stop the gospel going to the nations, and the souls of departed believers reign with Christ in heaven now.

The present age contains both the growth of the kingdom and continuing evil, wheat and tares together, with perhaps an intensification of opposition near the end. Christ will return once, visibly and bodily, at which point there will be a general resurrection of righteous and wicked, the final judgment, and the new heavens and new earth. The prefix a- is somewhat misleading: amillennialists do believe in a millennium, but not a future earthly one.

In City of God he interpreted the binding of Satan as accomplished by Christ, the thousand years as the church age, and the first resurrection as the spiritual resurrection of the soul, an interpretation that shaped Western theology for over a thousand years.

14115:
In the third and fourth centuries, theologians in Alexandria and then the Latin West grew uneasy with literal millenarian hopes, partly because of their association with Montanism and with materialistic expectations. Tyconius supplied a symbolic, ecclesial reading of Revelation, and Augustine, writing City of God after the sack of Rome in 410, gave it its classic form.

This reading became the majority view of the medieval Western church and of the magisterial Reformation. The Lutheran Augsburg Confession and the Reformed Second Helvetic Confession explicitly reject teaching of a worldly kingdom of the saints before the resurrection. Amillennialism remains the standard view in Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Lutheran and much Reformed theology, and it saw a revival among evangelicals in the late twentieth century.
